summary: The note is a seasonal guide to wildlife (mostly bird) watching spots, running from September through December 2023. Each location is tied to a time of year and a featured species, with a quote from a local naturalist, photographer or enthusiast. The spots range from marshes and fields to cliffs, a pond, an estuary, a ridge, woods and a valley.
one_line: A seasonal guide to eight bird-watching locations from September to December, each with an expert's quote and featured species.
key_facts: The guide opens with autumn after September 1, 2023, presenting wildlife watching as a calming escape from modern life.
Marshlands Conservatory, visited on September 5, has reeds and ponds and draws migratory birds, herons and kingfishers; naturalist Emma Clarkson is quoted there.
Harmony Fields hosts meadowlarks and skylarks singing at dawn in mid-September; local bird enthusiast James Whitman says the dawn 'symphony' stirs the soul.
Falcon's Cliff offers peregrine falcons performing aerial displays on the weekend of the 24th in late September; ornithologist Sarah Bennett describes the scene.
Twilight Pond becomes a gathering place for herons in October at dusk; photographer Isabelle Harwood talks about capturing the fleeting connection between light, water and flight.
Observers at Twilight Pond bring tripods and cameras to photograph herons at dusk.
The River's Mouth estuary, visited in October, mixes fresh and saltwater and attracts ducks, sandpipers, sea birds and river fowl; marine biologist Nathan Garcia is quoted.
Eagle's Ridge, visited in November, requires an ascent to see soaring eagles; climber and birdwatcher Liam Stone says an eagle sometimes glides close enough to see the glint in its eye.
Moonshadow Woods offers owl watching on late November evenings; Luna Fletcher, a watcher and owlet rescuer, speaks of the wisdom in their silence.
Songbird Valley is a December destination for chickadees, finches and nuthatches; local musician Theo Nguyen likens their calls to notes on nature's scale.
